etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English withinne, withinnen, from Old English wiþinnan; equivalent to with +‎ in.

definitions.definition: In the inner part, spatially; physically inside.

quote.citation: 1908 October, Kenneth Grahame, The Wind in the Willows, New York, N.Y.: Charles Scribner’s Sons, →OCLC:
quote.text: The Rat […]  lightly stepped into a little boat which the Mole had not observed. It was painted blue outside and white within, and was just the size for two animals; and the Mole's whole heart went out to it at once […] .

definitions.definition: In the scope or range of.

quote.citation: 2011, Tom Fordyce, Rugby World Cup 2011: England 12-19 France‎[1]:
quote.text: England struck back with a fine try from Ben Foden and closed to within seven points with three minutes left when Mark Cueto capitalised on a break from replacement Matt Banahan.

quote.citation: 2012, Christoper Zara, Tortured Artists: From Picasso and Monroe to Warhol and Winehouse, the Twisted Secrets of the World's Most Creative Minds, part 1, chapter 1, 27:
quote.text: On October 6, 1927, Warner Bros. released The Jazz Singer, the first sound-synched feature film, prompting a technological shift of unprecedented speed and unstoppable force. Within two years, nearly every studio release was a talkie.

quote.citation: 2012 June 9, Owen Phillips, “Euro 2012: Netherlands 0-1 Denmark”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: And Netherlands, backed by a typically noisy and colourful travelling support, started the second period in blistering fashion and could have had four goals within 10 minutes

definitions.definition: In or into the interior; inside.
(law) In the context of which the present document or ruling is made.

quote.citation: 2013, Court of Appeal for Ontario, Malka v. Vasiliadis:
quote.text: As part of the within appeal the appellants brought a fresh evidence motion. Although the court did not specifically address the motion in its oral reasons dismissing the appeal, that motion was rejected by the court for the following reasons.
